blocks.text: Chapter 7.
Probabilistic Thinking: Bayes, Fat Tails, and Asymmetry
Seventh night, friend — and it opens in a London office in 1941, where a woman decides who might die.

Her name is Vera Atkins, intelligence officer for the French Section of Britain's Special Operations Executive. Her job: recruit and deploy spies into Nazi-occupied France. There is no playbook. From an interview and fragments of a biography she must judge whether a candidate's French, temperament, and nerve give them a fighting chance undercover — knowing a wrong call means torture and death, and even a right call carries terrible odds. Of the roughly 400 agents F Section sent into France, about 100 never came back.

Certainty was never on the table, friend. What Atkins could do was estimate: weigh each factor, assign rough likelihoods, deploy where the expected value justified the risk — and update relentlessly as radio traffic and safe-house reports came in. After the war, she crossed Europe tracing the fates of her missing agents until she had accounted for every one — closing the feedback loop on her own decisions. That is tonight's tool: thinking in likelihoods when proof is impossible. The world, from where any of us stands, is a fog of chance and partial information — and the person who estimates well beats the person who waits for certainty.
Evidence means nothing without your priors

Thomas Bayes was an eighteenth-century English minister whose posthumous essay seeded one of the most useful ideas humans possess: the meaning of new information depends on what you already knew. Hold priors — probability estimates built from existing knowledge — and revise them incrementally as evidence arrives, instead of treating each new fact as a verdict from nowhere.
Pause and guess: A headline announces: "Violent crime in your city DOUBLED last year." Sounds like a reason to move. What single question defuses the headline — and what's the Bayesian answer?
Ready? Here is what happened.

"What was the base rate?" If violent crime ran at one incident per 10,000 residents, then "doubled" means... two per 10,000 — still vanishingly rare. And your prior knowledge that violent crime has trended downward for decades should dampen the update even further. Without the base rate, the headline manipulates you. With it, the headline barely moves you. Two disciplines keep the method honest, friend: remember that priors are themselves estimates with error bars — hold them open to revision, or "updating" collapses into confirming what you already believed; and interrogate every new data point with the Bayesian question: what do I already know that determines how much this should change my mind? One more tool for the kit — conditional probability: ask whether events are independent or dependent before trusting your intuition. A die has no memory — a run of sixes says nothing about the next roll (believing otherwise is the gambler's fallacy). But draw cards without replacement and every draw reshapes the odds of the next. Before you compute anything, friend, ask: has the deck been reshuffled?
The room where the average dies

Most of us picture probability as the bell curve: outcomes cluster around a meaningful average, extremes fall off fast and are physically capped. Human height fits — the average hovers near five-foot-seven, and no one will ever walk in at fifty feet tall. In bell-curve domains, the average tells you most of what you need, and planning around it works.

Pause and guess: Now run the book's thought experiment. A room holds a hundred ordinary people. First add the TALLEST person on Earth. Then instead add the RICHEST person on Earth. What happens to the room's averages — and why does the difference matter more than almost anything in statistics?
Ready? Here is what happened.

The tallest man barely nudges the average height — he's maybe 40% above the mean, and physics caps him there. But add the world's richest person and the room's average wealth becomes meaningless — he isn't 40% above the average, friend; he's hundreds of thousands of times it. That's a fat-tailed distribution: no cap on the extreme, outliers thousands or millions of times the typical — and the domains that run this way are exactly the ones that matter: wealth, market moves, wars, pandemics, book sales, technology adoption. In fat tails, the rare outlier doesn't skew the numbers — it dominates them: total wartime deaths are driven by the few largest wars; total market returns by a handful of extreme days. So think in orders of magnitude — not "a bit above or below average?" but "which power of ten am I in?" And draw the strategic conclusion, friend, because it changes everything: in a bell-curve world you can forecast, since tomorrow resembles the distribution of yesterdays. In a fat-tailed world, the most consequential event may be unlike anything in your data — so precise prediction is a mug's game. You will not foresee the specific crash or breakthrough. What you can do is position yourself so extremes can't ruin you — and ideally pay you. Know which kind of domain you're standing in before you trust any average.
The tilt in your own estimates

Third pillar, friend — and it points the telescope at yourself. Asymmetry, or metaprobability: the probability that your probability estimates are any good. It's not enough to produce a number; you need a view on your own calibration — and human miscalibration is rarely symmetric. Our errors bunch on one side — almost always the optimistic one. Investors confidently projecting 20%-plus annual returns realize far less — and virtually no one under-promises and over-delivers by the margin the optimists over-promise. Even arrival times tilt: traffic and lost keys can add twenty minutes; almost nothing subtracts twenty. When the deviations from your estimate are lopsided, shift the estimate toward the heavy side — and drop your confidence. The discipline is to keep two books: one on the odds of the event, one on the odds that you've judged the odds well. Track your record, find your habitual miss direction, and correct like a marksman correcting for wind.

And then build for the fog rather than against it. Nassim Taleb's word is antifragility: beyond surviving shocks — a position that improves when volatility and extremes hit. Two construction rules, friend. Seek upside optionality: situations where the downside is small and capped, the upside large and open-ended — the networking evening that costs three hours and might change a career; cheap experiments; small side bets. Many tiny losses, occasional enormous wins — the hundredth bet pays for the ninety-nine. And fail properly: never take a risk that can wipe you out — survival is the precondition for ever collecting a tail event — and extract the lesson from every cheap miss so the next bet is better calibrated. Vera Atkins ran F Section exactly this way: she couldn't predict which network would collapse — she estimated, updated, spread risk across many operations, and kept the organization able to absorb losses and continue. Probabilistic thinking never promised her certainty, friend. It promised better decisions than paralysis or blind confidence — and over hundreds of decisions, better odds compound into victory.
Before you go

So: Atkins decided lives on estimates and closed every feedback loop; Bayes says evidence only means something against your priors and base rates; the richest man in the room murders the average, and fat tails demand preparation over prediction; your errors lean optimistic, so keep two books and correct for your personal wind; and the antifragile position — capped downside, open upside, no bet that can kill you — turns the fog itself into an ally.

One night remains in this book, friend — and it's a gift of three blades. Three thinking shortcuts so sharp that each fits in a sentence, yet each can save you years: the trick of solving problems backwards — asking not "how do I succeed?" but "what would guarantee failure?"; the rule that the simplest explanation usually wins; and the razor that saves relationships — why you should almost never explain by malice what stupidity explains perfectly well. Next time, the finale: the three razors — inversion, Occam, and Hanlon.
Key takeaways
Probabilistic thinking: estimate likelihoods with math and logic when certainty is impossible — the good estimator beats the proof-waiter.
Bayes: new evidence only means something against priors and base rates — "doubled" from 1-in-10,000 is still 2-in-10,000.
Check independence first: dice have no memory, decks without replacement do — ask if the deck was reshuffled.
Fat tails: the richest man in the room destroys the average — in wealth, markets, wars and pandemics, the outlier IS the story.
In fat-tailed domains, stop forecasting and start positioning: prepare for shocks you cannot name.
Asymmetry and antifragility: your errors skew optimistic, so keep two books — and structure bets with capped downside, open upside, and no ruin.
